metadata.file_name: Feeling bad and doing bad  student confidence in reading in rural China.pdf
metadata.title: Feeling bad and doing bad: student confidence in reading in rural China

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study combines authors’ own rural China survey data (grade 4 students from 135 rural primary schools) with PIRLS cross-country comparison results for 45 countries/regions. The rural-China analyses are estimated using an OLS regression framework with county fixed effects and Huber–White standard errors corrected for class-level clustering, but the manuscript does not report the use of PIRLS sampling weights or any explicit student/school weight variables. Because the paper does not describe applying complex survey weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) and instead relies on robust clustered standard errors, the results should be interpreted as conditional associations within the sampled rural schools rather than fully population-representative estimates. For replication with PIRLS microdata, analysts should use the official PIRLS student sampling weights and replicate weights when estimating cross-country comparisons, and should align the clustering level (class/school) with the PIRLS design.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables in this paper are (i) a PIRLS-based reading confidence scale score from questionnaire items and (ii) reading achievement measured using the authors’ own translated reading test items and reported standardized/skill-specific scores, rather than PV-based cognitive achievement scores. Because the paper does not report any explicit missing-data strategy (e.g., listwise deletion or imputation), the missing-data handling is a reporting gap. This matters because missingness in questionnaire items or test responses can affect scale scoring and regression estimates.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample for the rural-China regression analyses consists of 4,616 grade-4 students drawn from 135 rural primary schools in two provinces (Guizhou and Jiangxi), with three counties selected per province and up to two classes randomly selected per school. Students were included if they participated in the PIRLS-based reading confidence questionnaire and completed the 30-minute reading test constructed from the PIRLS item pool (translated following PIRLS guidelines), and if they had the relevant background and school/teacher variables used in the OLS model. The paper does not specify any additional exclusions (e.g., missing questionnaire items, incomplete test responses) or an explicit missing-data rule.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS 2011 Grade 4 Reading (cross-country comparison using PIRLS confidence scale and reading achievement)
main_findings.target_variable: Student reading confidence (PIRLS confidence scale score)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported as an ML metric; descriptive cross-country ranking: Rural China has 11% 'confident' readers and 68% 'somewhat confident' readers; average scale score 8.89 (lowest among listed countries/regions).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2011 Grade 4 Reading the study compared rural China against 45 other countries/regions on the PIRLS reading confidence scale and reading achievement, finding that rural China ranks last in student reading confidence (11% confident; average confidence scale score 8.89). This indicates that rural schooling contexts in China may systematically undermine students’ self-beliefs about reading, suggesting that reading-confidence interventions (e.g., improving access to books and strengthening reading instruction) should be prioritized in rural policy.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS 2011 Grade 4 Reading (authors’ rural China sample; grade 4 reading test and PIRLS confidence questionnaire)
main_findings.performance_metrics: OLS regression (Table 3, Column 1): Reading achievement (standardized) β=0.23***; Classroom library β=0.22*; School library 5,000+ books β=-0.11 (ns); Student gender β=0.29***; Math/Chinese test score β=0.17***; Fewer than 10 books at home β=-0.28***; Own room for study β=0.18***; R-squared=0.123; Observations=4,616.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2011 Grade 4 Reading data from rural China (4,616 grade-4 students), the study leveraged reading achievement, classroom library access, and home resource indicators to predict student reading confidence, finding that higher reading achievement is positively associated with confidence (β=0.23***) and that classroom libraries are also positively associated (β=0.22*). This indicates that improving both students’ reading skills and the immediate availability of books in classrooms may raise reading confidence, especially for students facing home resource constraints.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS 2011 Grade 4 Reading (authors’ rural China sample; tercile-split by reading achievement)
main_findings.target_variable: Student reading confidence (heterogeneous associations by reading achievement terciles)
main_findings.performance_metrics: OLS regression by terciles (Table 3): Reading achievement β=0.21*** (top), 0.27* (middle), 0.43*** (bottom). Classroom library β=0.12 (top), 0.13 (middle), 0.43*** (bottom). Key reading skills taught at grade 4+ β=-0.14* (top), -0.04 (middle), 0.01 (bottom). Teacher reading training (16+ hours) β=-0.03 (top), -0.25* (middle), -0.03 (bottom). Uses children’s books β=0.13* (top), 0.01 (middle), -0.09 (bottom). R-squared: 0.060 (top), 0.084 (middle), 0.098 (bottom).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2011 Grade 4 Reading data from rural China, the study leveraged reading achievement and school/teacher factors to predict reading confidence separately for top, middle, and bottom reading-ability terciles, finding that the confidence–achievement link is strongest for weaker readers (β=0.43*** in the bottom tercile) and that classroom library access is especially associated with confidence among weak readers (β=0.43***). This indicates that rural reading policies should target book access in classrooms and early skill-building for low-achieving readers, since confidence gains appear most responsive in this subgroup.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses PIRLS 2011 Grade 4 reading instruments as a basis for a rural China survey conducted in May 2015, sampling 4,616 students from 135 rural primary schools in Guizhou and Jiangxi. It compares rural China to 45 other PIRLS participating countries/regions on reading confidence and reading achievement, reporting that rural China ranks last in confidence (11% confident; average confidence scale score 8.89) and also last in reading achievement (overall scale score 0.23; retrieving 0.33; interpreting 0.10). Within rural China, the authors estimate OLS models predicting reading confidence from reading achievement, access to books (especially classroom libraries), teacher characteristics, teaching practices, and student/home controls, with class-level clustered robust standard errors. The key quantitative associations are positive for reading achievement (β=0.23***) and classroom libraries (β=0.22*), and stronger among bottom reading terciles (reading achievement β=0.43***; classroom library β=0.43***). Limitations include the absence of any reported missing-data strategy and no explicit use of PIRLS sampling/replicate weights.
